# Retrieving Wikipedia Content and Extracting Claim-Relevant Passages: The Evidence-Extraction Workflow for Fact Verification

**Scope note.** The request did not specify particular Wikipedia articles or a particular factual claim, so this report documents the established research methodology for exactly that operation — retrieving Wikipedia article content and extracting the passages that directly address (support, refute, or fail to address) a factual claim — including the formal task definition, the systems that perform it, the benchmarks that evaluate it, and the programmatic means of accessing Wikipedia content.

---

## 1. Formal task definition

The canonical formulation is **FEVER (Fact Extraction and VERification)** [1]. Given a claim *c* and a processed English Wikipedia corpus, a system must (a) retrieve the Wikipedia evidence for the claim and (b) decide its truth value, via three sub-tasks:

1. **Document retrieval** — identify the Wikipedia pages containing evidence;
2. **Evidence (sentence) retrieval** — select the specific sentences within those pages;
3. **Label prediction (aggregation)** — classify the claim as **SUPPORTS**, **REFUTES**, or **NOT ENOUGH INFO (NEI)**.

Formally, evidence for a claim is a set of *evidence groups*, each a set of (page, sentence-line) tuples. A group is *sufficient* if the claim can be inferred from it alone; a claim is SUPPORTS/REFUTES if at least one sufficient group exists in the gold evidence, and NEI if no such evidence exists in Wikipedia. Retrieval therefore operates at **(page title, sentence index) granularity**, not free-text spans [1].

**Corpus.** FEVER uses the 2016-12-21 English Wikipedia dump with tables, infoboxes, lists, and other boilerplate removed; pages are split into passages and then sentences (~5.4M evidence candidates) [1].

## 2. How gold "claim-addressing passages" are annotated

Claims were crowdsourced by mutating sentences from intro sections of popular Wikipedia pages, with intended labels: **SUPPORTED** (copy/paraphrase, meaning preserved), **REFUTED** (entity substitution, negation, numeral/date perturbation), **NEI** (substitution with an entity not covered by the page). For REFUTED/NEI claims, separate annotators located the minimal supporting/refuting sentences — evidence can span multiple sentences and pages (multi-hop) — and an independent annotator, shown only the claim plus the annotated evidence, had to reproduce the intended label; failures were discarded or re-annotated. The result: ~185,445 claims (≈145,433 train / 19,958 dev / 6,666 test; train distribution ≈55% SUPPORTS, 25% REFUTES, 20% NEI) [1][2].

## 3. The pipeline: from article retrieval to extracted passages

**Stage 1 — Document retrieval.** The FEVER baseline uses TF-IDF/BM25 term matching (Elasticsearch-style) [1]; FEVER claims are entity-centric, so lexical retrieval is a strong baseline. Later work adds dense bi-encoders fine-tuned on FEVER evidence with hard negatives, typically hybridized with BM25 plus cross-encoder re-ranking [17]. Notably, dense retrievers trained on QA-style data **underperform BM25 on entity-centric claims** unless trained in-domain [18].

**Stage 2 — Sentence-level evidence extraction.** The baseline ranks sentences of retrieved pages by TF-IDF cosine similarity with the claim and keeps the top-k (≈5) [1]. Neural variants score claim–sentence pairs with BERT cross-encoders; **UKP-Athene** fine-tunes ESIM for 3-way claim–sentence entailment and keeps sentences above an entailment-probability threshold — the strongest 2019-era selector [7].

**Stage 3 — Evidence aggregation.** Because claims often need multiple sentences across documents, aggregation over the extracted passages matters as much as extraction:

| System | Aggregation approach | Dev acc. | Blind test |
|---|---|---|---|
| FEVER baseline [1] | feed-forward NN over claim–sentence reps | ≈55% | ≈51% |
| GEAR [5] | fully-connected graph over evidence sentences, graph attention | 66.7% | – |
| GEAR^bar [5] | learned aggregation over per-sentence verdicts | 67.6% | – |
| HAN/MAHN [4] | joint multi-hop attention, iterative evidence accumulation | ≈67% | – |
| KGAT [6] | word-level graph; Gaussian-kernel attention over cosine-similarity bands | 69.8% | 70.6% |
| UKP-Athene [7][8] | ESIM entailment-probability aggregation | ≈71.5% | **74.5%** |

Aggregation/reasoning over evidence yields roughly **+11–14 points** over the baseline under identical lexical retrieval; better sentence selection adds several more. Later work moved to semantic-level graphs [20], end-to-end BERT-era pipelines (≈75–76% blind test), and KILT-style unified retrieval+verification [19]. NEI handling is implicit: systems must abstain when no supporting/refuting evidence is retrieved.

## 4. Evaluation metrics for extracted evidence

Official scoring (`fever-scorer`) [2][3]:

- **Document retrieval:** page-level Recall@5 (an upper bound downstream).
- **Evidence precision/recall/F1:** per claim over (page, line) tuples with exact matching against the union of gold evidence groups; macro-averaged. **NEI claims are excluded** (no gold evidence exists).
- **Label accuracy:** fraction of correct 3-way labels.
- **FEVER score (primary end-to-end metric):** a claim counts as correct **only if the label is correct AND the submitted evidence is sufficient**, operationalized as evidence F1 ≥ θ = 0.05 — penalizing systems that guess the right label from wrong or insufficient passages [1][3].

## 5. Benchmarks beyond FEVER

- **FEVER 2.0 (adversarial).** Humans wrote claims designed to fool top systems (GEORGE, GEAR, UKP-Athene, BERT baseline) against the same Wikipedia dump; ~963 validated claims. Every system dropped 10–20 accuracy points (best: GEORGE ≈57.6% vs ≈67% on standard test); a large share fooled all four systems. Most effective attacks: numerical/date reasoning, entity substitution, subtle negation, multi-hop evidence, and lexical-overlap bias. **Evidence retrieval was the major bottleneck** — systems frequently retrieved wrong or insufficient passages even when decisive evidence existed [9][10][11].
- **AVeriTeC (2024).** ~4,000 real-world claims from professional fact-checks; systems return a yes/no answer plus supporting evidence as (question, answer, URL) triples against live web/Wikipedia evidence. Primary metric is human evaluation on three criteria (answer correct? evidence relevant? evidence supports the answer?), scored 1/0.5/0. Retrieval-augmented LLM pipelines won; the organizer baseline scored ≈0.35 [12][13].
- **SciFact.** 1,409 expert-written scientific claims verified against 5,183 S2ORC abstracts with sentence-level rationales; three-stage pipeline (retrieve abstracts → select rationale sentences → verdict), combined F1 metric; top systems ≈0.62. Incorporated into BEIR, where BM25 outperformed many out-of-domain dense retrievers [14][15].
- **CLEF CheckThat! (2018–2025).** Full pipeline: check-worthiness, previously-fact-checked-claim detection, web evidence retrieval, verdict prediction; multilingual (Arabic, English, Spanish, Bulgarian, etc.); metrics F1, MAP/MRR/nDCG; dominant approaches fine-tuned transformers, with LLM/RAG pipelines common from 2023 [16].

## 6. Wikipedia structure as evidence

- **Entity linking and hyperlinks.** Anchor-text links provide distant supervision for entity linking (AIDA, TAGME, BLINK, GENRE, LUKE) [37–41]; entity annotations serve as query-side anchors for title-based document retrieval, alias/redirect expansion, graph edges for hop retrieval, and stable provenance anchors. UKP-Athene combined entity linking with Wikipedia search; multi-hop attention networks used entity-linking retrieval plus one-hop hyperlink expansion. Datasets built from hyperlinks (WikiHop, 2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA) and entity-graph retrievers (DFGN, PathRetriever, HopRetriever — the latter specifically for multi-hop fact verification) exploit the link graph directly. Failure modes: claims with no named entities, disambiguation cascades, and hyperlink sparsity for long-tail entities [42–45]. **KILT** unifies fact-checking, multi-hop QA, slot filling (T-REx, aligned to Wikidata triples), and entity-linking subtasks on one 5.9M-page snapshot, requiring provenance for all tasks [19]. **FEVEROUS** extends evidence to structured tables and lists [46].
- **Tables.** TabFact (~120k claims over ~16k Wikipedia tables), InfoTabs (tables + reference text), HybridQA (multi-hop across tables and hyperlinked passages), OTTer (open-domain tabular fact-checking with retrieval); TAPAS/TAPEX are specialized verifiers [21–24].
- **Revision history.** Static snapshots mis-evaluate systems as Wikipedia evolves. **VitaminC** mined revisions to build ~400k contrastive claim–evidence pairs where an edit flips factuality; **Fool Me Twice** writes adversarial claims against *current* articles to expose evidence drift; WikiContradiction targets self-contradictions from asynchronous edits; WikiTrust and ORES provide provenance-based reliability signals [25–27].
- **Citations.** The "Citation Needed" corpus (~150k sentences annotated for lacking support), CiteWorth (citation-worthiness), WikiPassageQA (claim support as passage retrieval from cited sources), the WikiCite initiative (machine-readable citation metadata in Wikidata), and citation-quality studies flagging retracted/predatory references [28–31].
- **LLM-era factuality.** **FActScore** decomposes long-form generations into atomic facts and verifies each against Wikipedia biographies; **SAFE** automates this with search; grounding checkers (AlignScore, MiniCheck) and systems like WikiChat and RefChecker verify claims against retrieved Wikipedia content [32–36].

## 7. Programmatic access to Wikipedia article content

| Channel | Best for | Format | Freshness |
|---|---|---|---|
| MediaWiki Action API | Targeted queries, revisions, wikitext | JSON (wikitext/HTML/extracts) | Live |
| REST API | Summaries, rendered HTML, pageviews | JSON / HTML | Live |
| Dumps | Full-corpus, reproducible research | XML (wikitext), JSON, SQL | Snapshot (~2×/month) |
| DBpedia | RDF triples, entity linking | RDF / SPARQL | Release-based |
| Wikidata | Structured facts, cross-lingual entity IDs | SPARQL / JSON | Live + dumps |

The Action API returns raw wikitext (`prop=revisions&rvslots=main&rvprop=content`), plain-text extracts (`prop=extracts`), or rendered HTML (`action=parse`); batch up to 50 titles per request, paginate with `continue`, set a descriptive User-Agent, and use `maxlag` for polite crawling [47]. Dumps include `pages-articles.xml.bz2` (multistream with index), full revision history, CirrusSearch JSON dumps, and Wikidata entity dumps [48]. DBpedia offers a SPARQL endpoint, Spotlight entity annotation, and NIF corpora with character offsets for passage-level work [49]; Wikidata provides QIDs as stable cross-lingual entity keys [50].

**Passage-extraction tooling:** wikiextractor (dump → plain text), gensim WikiCorpus, mwparserfromhell/wikitextparser (surgical wikitext parsing), Parsoid for boilerplate-stripped HTML [51][52]. **Ready-made passage corpora:** DPR's `psgs_w100.tsv` (21M 100-word passages from the 2016-12-21 dump) [53], the KILT knowledge source (5.9M articles, 2019-08-01) [19], Pyserini/Anserini prebuilt BM25 and dense indexes [54], and Hugging Face `wikimedia/wikipedia` streaming datasets [55].

**Reproducibility and licensing:** API content is live and mutable — pin to dated dumps or record page/revision IDs and Wikidata QIDs, and report snapshot dates. Wikipedia text is CC BY-SA (new revisions CC BY-SA 4.0 since 2023), so attribution and share-alike apply to redistribution [56]; Wikimedia Enterprise serves high-volume structured access [57].

## 8. Cross-cutting findings

1. **Extraction granularity is sentence-level provenance**, not free-text spans — evidence is scored by exact (page, line) matching [1][3].
2. **Retrieval is the bottleneck**: adversarial evaluation showed systems fail most often by retrieving wrong or insufficient passages, not by mis-reading them [9]; dense retrievers can underperform BM25 on entity-centric claims [18].
3. **Aggregation over extracted passages adds double-digit gains** under identical retrieval [5][6].
4. **Static snapshots mis-evaluate systems** as Wikipedia evolves; revision-aware construction (VitaminC, Fool Me Twice) is the main mitigation [25][26].
5. **Evidence reliability is not uniform** — citation-quality issues and table incompleteness are recurring limitations [28][31].
